walkthroughs.body_html:
There's verbal irony (saying the opposite), situational irony (the outcome is unexpected) and dramatic irony (the audience knows more than the character).

Birling calling the Titanic "unsinkable" is dramatic irony.

Sibilance creates intimacy or menace; anaphora builds rhythm and urgency.

Naming these precisely beats writing "repetition" — and examiners notice.

Zoomorphism turns humans into animals — Macbeth becomes a hunted beast.

Bathos drops the tone suddenly. Adding these to your toolkit signals real expertise.

mcqs.q: When the audience knows something a character doesn't, this is:
options: verbal irony
dramatic irony
situational irony
bathos

mcqs.q: Giving animal traits to humans is:
options: personification
zoomorphism
anthropomorphism
pathetic fallacy

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a theme and a symbol?
options: A theme is an abstract idea or concern the text explores (e.g. mortality); a symbol is a concrete image that stands for something else (e.g. a skull).
Dramatic irony is when characters speak in dramatic voices.
Themes are just symbols repeated through the book.
A theme is the title of the book.
Dramatic irony is when characters speak in dramatic voices.
Verbal irony is when you make a joke about something.
Dramatic irony is when something ironic happens in a play.
When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension between the character's words/actions and the audience's understanding.
Verbal irony is when you make a joke about something.
Verbal irony is just saying something unexpected.
A theme is the title of the book.
When a speaker says one thing but means another — typically the opposite — relying on shared context for the listener to detect the gap.
